newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Budget nerves haunt market.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Budget nerves haunt market.

text.p: UK gilts will hover nervously around present levels until the budget on Wednesday, after that it depends on the extent of the fiscal tightening, analysts said on Monday.
"We are in for a quiet time before the budget because everyone will be sitting around on the sidelines," said Merrill Lynch gilts analyst Steven Andrew.

"If we have tightening of more than three to five billion stg ($5-8.3 billion) then it is good for the gilts market, if it is any less we are going to see a negative reaction because it will anticipate higher rates."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will deliver the Labour Party's first budget in almost 20 years. Most analysts are expecting he will take approximately three to four billion pounds out of the economy.
"The budget will take centre stage and set the direction for the week," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson bond analysts Steve Scott.

"Our economists suggest the tax rises might be lower than the forecast...3-4 billion," he said, thereby increasing the likelihood of an interest rise from the Bank of England after its monetary policy committee meeting ending on July 10.
Once the budget was out of the way, some analysts predicted the gilts spread against Bunds would come in to around 100 basis points from its current level of 150.
But much of the gains would be down to Bund underperformance, they said.

Gilts and short sterling were off on Monday after higher than expected consumer credit figures. The September gilt future sold off early and was down 11/32 at 114-04, while the September short sterling contract was three basis points lower at 92.91.

Most analysts felt the Bank of England would be compelled to raise interest rates, whatever Brown did, in order to stem the robust growth in consumer spending. Bank of England figures out on Monday showed consumer credit leapt by 1.105 billion stg in May while April's rise was revised upwards significantly.

Market speculation about the budget has centred on a few policies including the reduction or abolition of Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT), increases in property stamp duty or the reduction in mortgage interest relief, and various corporation taxes.
There was also the possibility of a rise in some excise duties and the restriction of certain personal allowances, some analysts said.
Analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expected the levies to total 3-4 billion sterling, split fairly evenly between the corporate and the personal sector.
"The key question is how much," they said.

"It is one of the most eagerly awaited budgets for a while as nobody really knows what is going to be in it and the extent to any reorganisation of the public finances and tax rates," Andrew said. "There is much speculation."
"The implications for the gilts market are not as strong as they are for the equities market," he added, saying that many eventualities had been priced in.
A cut in ACT will hit the stock market as the major funds and institutions will be able to claim less tax back on their equity holdings as a result.
Scott said the budget would also reveal a little more about the state of the government finances. "There might not be as big a black hole as some are thinking,"
Monday's credit figures certainly increased the pressure on Brown to raise personal taxes, or risk interest rates going sky-high.
"It reinforces the need for further tightening policy, the question is whether it is monetary tightening or fiscal tightening," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale.
Analysts said there were few other economic figures or events during the week that would hold any marked significance for the market.
June's purchasing managers index, out on Tuesday and usually a key indicator for manufacturing, will be overshadowed by Brown's budget.

The Confederation of British Industry's latest distributive trades survey, due on Thursday, will provide yet more evidence of the pace of high street spending. But last month, the survey painted a much weaker picture than official sales figures, which leapt 1.1 percent in May. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
